conflicts.point: Whether statutory pre-deployment licensing gates act as protective safeguards against systemic tail risks or as regressive regulatory moats that entrench incumbent monopolies.

positions.stance: Statutory pre-deployment gates impose prohibitive fixed compliance costs that protect dominant market incumbents and crush decentralized open-source development.
Mandatory pre-deployment gates are essential institutional safeguards to prevent irreversible catastrophic deployments by halting unaligned systems before activation.

conflicts.point: Whether ex-post revenue penalties and real-time telemetry provide sufficient deterrence or merely function as manageable operational costs for dominant firms.

positions.stance: Real-time output telemetry paired with revenue-scaled liability creates an adaptive governance model that holds actors financially accountable for measurable harms without stalling innovation.
Revenue-scaled liability acts as an ex-post forensic audit mechanism that cannot reverse irreversible systemic failures or constrain entities too big to fail.

verdicts.conflict: Whether statutory pre-deployment licensing gates act as protective safeguards against systemic tail risks or as regressive regulatory moats that entrench incumbent monopolies.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist position supported by C1 and C2 prevails on empirical specificity because hardware infrastructure data confirms that capital expenditures exceeding one billion dollars per cluster create a natural oligopoly. This economic reality demonstrates that fixed compliance costs disproportionately burden smaller entrants regardless of whether pre-deployment gates are necessary for risk mitigation.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence showing that small laboratories routinely deploy frontier systems under statutory gate regimes without market exit would weaken the accelerationist claim.

verdicts.conflict: Whether ex-post revenue penalties and real-time telemetry provide sufficient deterrence or merely function as manageable operational costs for dominant firms.
verdicts.rationale: The safetyist position represented by C5 accounts for the structural asymmetry between corporate balance sheets and regulatory fines, whereas C4 assumes linear financial accountability without addressing entities too big to fail. Revenue-scaled penalties on trillion-dollar firms frequently function as variable operating expenses rather than binding constraints on deployment decisions.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Empirical demonstration that revenue-scaled liability successfully halts deployment in firms capitalized above one trillion dollars would validate the accelerationist framework.
